content: Linoleic acid (LA) is an unsaturated omega-6 fatty acid that exists as a colorless liquid. In scientific terms, it is referred to as 18:2(n-6). Structurally, linoleic acid is a carboxylic acid composed of an 18-carbon chain with two cis double bonds. The first double bond is positioned at the sixth carbon from the omega (methyl) end of the molecule. The term linoleic is derived from the Greek word linon, meaning flax, while oleic refers to its association with oil or oleic acid. If the omega-6 double bond is removed, linoleic acid is converted into oleic acid. From a physiological perspective, linoleic acid is classified as a polyunsaturated fatty acid and plays a critical role in the biosynthesis of prostaglandins. It is a key component of the lipids found in cell membranes. Linoleic acid is particularly abundant in various vegetable oils, such as safflower oil and sunflower oil. For the body to fully utilize linoleic acid, it must first be converted into gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) through a reaction catalyzed by the enzyme delta-6-desaturase (D6D). Linoleic acid belongs to the group of essential fatty acids known as omega-6 fatty acids, which are vital dietary components for all mammals. Another essential fatty acid group is the omega-3 fatty acids, such as alpha-linolenic acid. A deficiency in omega-6 fatty acids can lead to symptoms such as dry hair, hair loss, and impaired wound healing. However, it is relatively easy to meet the daily requirement for omega-6 fatty acids, even for individuals on low-fat diets. Consuming approximately one tablespoon of polyunsaturated plant oils per day is sufficient to fulfill this requirement. Linoleic acid also has various industrial applications. It is used in the production of soaps, emulsifiers, and quick-drying oils. When linoleic acid undergoes reduction, it forms linoleyl alcohol. In recent years, linoleic acid has gained popularity in the beauty and skincare industry due to its beneficial effects on the skin. Research has demonstrated that linoleic acid, when applied topically, exhibits anti-inflammatory properties, helps reduce acne, and enhances moisture retention in the skin. Noni seed oil, which is rich in linoleic acid, is a common ingredient in many beauty products. Linoleic acid is present in a wide range of oils and foods. Examples include safflower oil (78% linoleic acid), poppy seed oil (70%), walnut oil, grass-fed cow milk, olive oil, palm oil, sunflower oil, soybean oil, lard, coconut oil, egg yolks (16%), spirulina, peanut oil, okra, rice bran oil, wheat germ oil, grape seed oil, macadamia oil, pistachio oil, and sesame oil.
